lines.text: In 1970, on a frozen peninsula in the far north of Russia, Soviet engineers began to drill a hole straight down.
The hole was narrower than a dinner plate, and they kept drilling for almost twenty years.
The deeper they went, the hotter the rock became, until it behaved more like plastic than stone, and the drill could go no further.
The hole was meant to reach the boundary beneath the Earth's crust. It never even came close.
Final depth: a little over twelve kilometres. The deepest hole ever dug.
And yet, on the scale of the whole planet, it is barely a scratch.
The centre of the Earth lies more than six thousand kilometres below our feet.
No one has ever been there. No one ever will. So how do we know what is down there?
We cannot dig to it, we cannot see through it, and we cannot send a probe down into it.
Yet today we can draw the inside of the Earth layer by layer: a thin crust, a thick mantle, an ocean of liquid metal… and at the centre, a solid ball as hot as the surface of the Sun.
That picture came from four clues — and the most important of them came from the planet's worst moments.
Our first clue is a weight.
In 1798, in an outbuilding at his house in London, Henry Cavendish set out to weigh the world.
Not with a scale — you cannot put a planet on a scale — but by measuring how strongly lead attracts lead.
Inside, he hung a rod from a fine wire, with a small lead ball at each end, and set two heavy lead balls close beside them.
To keep his own warmth from stirring the air, he watched from outside, through a telescope.
The heavy balls pulled on the small ones — gently, almost nothing — and the rod turned by a hair.
From that tiny turn, he worked out how strongly the whole Earth pulls… and so how heavy it must be.
The answer was strange. On average, the Earth was about five and a half times as dense as water.
But the rocks under our feet are only about half that dense.
So something deep inside had to be far heavier than rock.
In the 1890s, the German scientist Emil Wiechert suggested what it was: iron, like the iron meteorites that fall from the sky.
A heavy heart of metal. But it was only a guess. Nobody could look inside.
Clue two: the planet rings.
When a great earthquake strikes, it sends waves through the whole Earth, the way a struck bell sends sound through its metal.
Some waves push and squeeze, like sound. Others shake from side to side, like a rope being flicked.
And their speed depends on what they pass through: faster in hard, dense rock, slower in softer or hotter material.
By 1900, observatories around the world had seismographs: needles that drew every tremor on a turning drum of paper.
Each earthquake became a message, written in ink in many cities at once — but only for someone who could read it.
In 1897, a huge earthquake shook Assam, in north-eastern India.
Richard Dixon Oldham, of the Geological Survey of India, collected the records of its waves from stations around the globe.
Waves that crossed near the surface arrived on time. But waves that dived deep through the middle of the Earth came in late.
Like runners who hit mud in the middle of a race, they had passed through something different.
Something in the centre was slowing them down.
In 1906, Oldham published his conclusion: the Earth has a core.
Clue three: a wave that goes missing.
In 1909, an earthquake struck near Zagreb, and the Croatian scientist Andrija Mohorovičić noticed that its waves arrived twice.
Some came straight through the crust. But others dived a little deeper, into faster rock, and raced ahead.
He had found the bottom of the crust — only a few tens of kilometres down. Today it carries his name: the Moho.
Beneath that thin skin lies the mantle: hot, solid rock that slowly creeps, like very thick honey.
In 1914, Beno Gutenberg measured where the core begins: about two thousand nine hundred kilometres down.
Then seismologists noticed something stranger. The side-to-side waves never came through the core at all.
Those waves can travel through solids, but never through liquids.
So the core was liquid: an ocean of molten iron, thousands of kilometres deep.
And a liquid core, bending the waves like a lens, casts a shadow.
Waves bend whenever they enter a new material, just as a straw seems to bend in a glass of water.
On the far side of the planet from an earthquake, there is a ring where the main waves should never arrive.
But they did. Faint, ghostly ones. And nobody could explain them.
Clue four: a ghost in the shadow.
In Copenhagen, Inge Lehmann led the seismology department of Denmark's Geodetic Institute.
She was a patient, exact reader of squiggles on paper.
In 1929, a strong earthquake struck Buller, on New Zealand's South Island — on the far side of the world from Europe.
Its waves crossed the whole planet, and stations in Europe recorded them.
Lehmann studied the records. In the shadow zone, where nothing should arrive, faint waves had arrived.
Others called them noise, or waves that had bent around the edge of the core.
Lehmann tried another idea. Was the liquid core really liquid all the way through?
Suppose a smaller, solid ball sat at the very centre. It would catch those waves, bend them, and throw them into the shadow — exactly where they were seen.
She worked it out with pencil and paper, and kept her data on cards in old oatmeal boxes.
In 1936, at forty-eight, she published it. The title of her paper was a single symbol: P-prime.
Her idea was so simple it was easy to doubt. But within a few years, the leading seismologists had accepted it.
The Earth had an inner core.
Today we know that inner core is a ball of solid iron and nickel, about two thousand four hundred kilometres across.
It is about as hot as the surface of the Sun — and yet it is solid, squeezed by the weight of the whole planet above it.
Its heat is left over partly from the planet's birth, and partly made by radioactive atoms still decaying deep inside.
Around it, the liquid iron of the outer core keeps moving, and that motion makes the Earth's magnetic field.
The same field that turns a compass needle, and shields our air from the wind of the Sun.
The deepest place on our planet was found not by going there… but by listening.
And by a woman who kept working for decades after that discovery, and lived to be one hundred and four.
So — how do we know what is inside the Earth?
Its weight told us the middle is heavy. Its echoes told us there is a core.
A missing wave told us the core is liquid. And a ghost in the shadow told us that, at the very centre, it turns solid again.
Every big earthquake is still a lesson. Thousands of seismometers listen, and each wave adds a little more to the map.
The same trick now works on other worlds: a quake felt on another planet can reveal its heart too.
We will never stand at the centre of the Earth.
But we know its shape, its heat and its metal — because the planet keeps talking, and someone learned to listen.
